utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I apologise for a moment if you would excuse me. From that video 65 ter 40504, I would like to tender minutes from 24 to 25.49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, were you able to confirm that, whether those parts we saw yesterday were included in Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that they weren't included in the Prosecution exhibit shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we admit the Defence part separately? I think that should be possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, then the video shown yesterday will be admitted into Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1927, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, is it a fact that you were doing your job and helping people in Trnopolje and that fact helped you keep your job, you were not dismissed, or do you have another explanation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, nobody received an official dismissal. I was held in the camp like all the other inmates. I was brought there by force, I was kept there by force, I could not leave the camp, and I was not receiving my salary for that job. For that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were arrested along with the others, but do you have any explanation why your employment was not terminated?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who says it wasn't? Look at my payment lists. When was the last time I received my salary from the health centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But a formal decision was issued for others who were terminated in their employment. There is no such decision for you. Do you have any explanation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just gave you an explanation. My last salary that I received was in March and no more. From the camp I requested through the Serbian Red Cross the payment of the salaries that I had earned, and the answer that I received at the camp was: You're in the camp. You don't need your salary anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Doctor, you were no longer in Trnopolje. You went to join Cirkin and his unit in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not telling the truth. That did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the Serbian Red Cross arrive? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. That was the end of May, so sometime in the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of May the Serbian Red Cross arrived. Who specifically?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Curguz with another two ladies and also Dr. Dusko Ivic arrived. I don't know if he arrived with them, and Mico, a technician or an orderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your statements that you were able to go out, although it depended very much on the guards how easy it was to get out to look for medicines in surrounding settlements to bring them back for your patients?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's consistent with what I keep saying here. Trnopolje operated differently in different periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait, I'm answering your question now so hear me out, please. In different periods, different conditions prevailed. There were some periods there was no free movement at all. In other periods we had some degree of movement. It all depends on the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You associated that freedom of movement with the specific guards, not with various periods?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the entire western end of Republika Srpska and then the entire Republika Srpska was under very severe sanctions that affected medical institutions as well?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Republika Srpska did not exist, only Bosnia and Herzegovina existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave political debates aside. I'm talking about the area controlled by the Serbs. Was it under an embargo? The corridor was closed and all the other routes of supply were also compromised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly what territory was affected. I believe it was the entire region, not only the area populated by Serbs, but also areas populated by Muslims and Croats as well. As far as I know, Prijedor was inhabited not only by Serbs but also by Muslims. And if there were no medicines, they were not available to any of the ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not clear enough. I'm talking about the part of the territory controlled by the Serbs. Do you agree that what we now call the Muslim/Croat Federation was not under an embargo? Anything could be supplied via Dalmatia, whereas the situation was very different for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not control the borders. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Radojka Elankov is?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Elenkov. I heard the name but, I'm sorry, I can't give you any details. Mrs. Elenkov must have had a husband. I know a Dr. Elenkov who must have been her husband if you want to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was that doctor who was a Macedonian or a Bulgarian and she must be one of yours?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the names. I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Merhamet, the Muslim charity, was active in the Bosnian Krajina throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of Merhamet as a humanitarian organisation. Whether it was active throughout the war, I really couldn't tell you. You should make inquiries with them. It's easily verifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that Merhamet supplied medicines as part of their mission?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Merhamet was doing. They had no presence in the camp, and I don't believe the Serbs would have allowed them to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say they were not coming to Manjaca every week?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying Merhamet never came to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the regimen at Manjaca was stricter than in Trnopolje and Merhamet was there every week?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the regimen was stricter. I know it was a military barracks and it was all within the compound of the barracks, whereas the other camps in Prijedor, as opposed to Manjaca, which was linked to Banja Luka, those other camps were not controlled by the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D4609. I'm not sure if we have a translation yet. 1D4609.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the 13th July 1992 General Hospital Prijedor. They're sending a notification to the Merhamet charity, listing municipalities whose residents are receiving treatment at that hospital, which are Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi as well as a large number of refugees. And then it says below: [As read] "We have to emphasize that even before the conflict we were hard-up financially and in the current situation when we treat 150 Muslim patients daily whose treatment is not being paid for by anyone, may eventually disable us from providing medical assistance at all." And then it says: "We are addressing you as a charity to request that you organise and assist our institutions in terms of medicines, medical equipment, food, or money so that we could continue to help members of your ethnic community." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even before the war there were difficulties with medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said otherwise. The only thing is those medical supplies were not distributed equally among all the ethnic communities in the territories held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why are you saying that if you can't prove it? This text proves that you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in the Trnopolje camp where on the orders of the SDS ethnic cleansing was carried out, civilians were kept there for a few days and sent on, and there were great shortages of medical supplies. So, through Dr. Ivic and the Red Cross, I requested medicines but never received anything but anti-lice powder. It's absolutely impossible that there was no capacity of providing a single medicine to a camp where so many people were being victimised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By what?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By ethnic cleansing. The Serbian army rounded up people in the surrounding villages, brought them there, and then transported them in cattle wagons and other unsuitable transports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not nice of you to lie. Can Dr. Ivic confirm what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask Dr. Ivic. I requested from him personally those medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this notification, some sort of request from Merhamet, does it confirm that even the hospital was out of medicines?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything about the quantity of medicines available at the hospital or how they were supplied. I'm just saying that we in Trnopolje did not receive any medicines from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be received, MFI'd, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when you talk about that cleansing and bringing people in from villages, do you know that close to Trnopolje and close to Kozarac there were Muslim houses that had white cloths on their windows and people went on living and working a normal life for as long as they declared that they would not be involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact details, what happened outside the camp. I know that as time went by village after village and hamlet after hamlet had their populations expelled, if it was non-Serb population, that is, for as long as the war operations went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you know that there were armed Muslim groups in Prijedor, around Prijedor, all the way up until the end of 1994, that they lived in dug-outs, in the woods, they fought and killed peasants?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about any of those details. I know that there was resistance in certain places when Serbs wanted to take these villages. I heard that on one occasion an attempt was made to liberate Prijedor. That's the only information I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you, the few doctors that were there, received people from the entire area for medical treatment at your infirmary?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first people were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you accepted that and you treated them, irrespective of faith and ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I do to this day, invariably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see in this text that 100 Muslim patients are being treated daily at this department for internal medicine?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way of checking that. That's what this piece of paper says and I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a single location in Bosanska Krajina where a significant number of Muslims had not stayed on during the entire war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I tell you? How many Muslims stayed on in Prijedor, compare how many were there before the war and how many were there after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many were there during the war, can you tell us what the difference was between a Muslim who lived in Prijedor throughout and a Muslim who left for any reason, not to speculate? There were Muslims who were even in the Serb army and police and --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is in the following. During those years, they could not live peacefully in Prijedor. Often Serbs came to their houses and searched them, and in 1994, March 1994, actually, a few families were killed during the night, a husband, wife, all of them. Don't you remember? Don't you remember reading about that during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the reasons why some people fled, but how come some people managed to stay on throughout the war and as for this particular incident I issued an order to have it investigated in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this was a way the remaining small number of people who had stayed on were intimidated. This was aimed at getting them out of there because of this mistreatment on a daily basis and you forbade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you I'm the one who's talking now. These people had to stay because nobody could take them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Merdzanic, that Muslim extremists compiled lists of many Muslims and declared them traitors because they were not fighting against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Karadzic, that the Serbs also held Serbs in camp? Do you know that a Serb lady from Omarska, from the camp of Omarska stayed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We haven't got time --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am giving you answers, and when I'm giving these answers, you're supposed to keep quiet. I know that the Serbs kept their very own Serbs in the camp if they didn't want to do what they were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please, I am asking you whether you know about this. You and I do not need to engage in a debate. Just say whether you do know or you do not know?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some questions cannot be answered by I know or I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This one can. Do you know that the Muslims compiled a long list of Muslims who they declared traitors because they were not engaged in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that. This is the very first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the guards were not the ones who did something to people there, especially as far as rape is concerned, rather, it was people who came from the outside; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has to do with rape but not beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us finish with these beatings. You had not seen a single beating. You had not been beaten yourself. And you heard Serb guards shouting out there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. That is a total misinterpretation. The room where inmates were being beaten was within the infirmary. I personally examined the inmates who had been beaten and I talked to them. You don't really need to be that intelligent. As for someone to be present while the Serbs were beating other people, it's not that anyone was allowed to be there. I told you that I saw with my very own eyes when Zigic beat up an inmate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did say, didn't you, as far as rape was concerned, that there were seven reported rapes and that a woman who told you about this said to you that the rapist had threatened her, saying that she should not report that; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. I never said that the woman had made any threats or that the rapist had made threats or whatever. A few women agreed to be examined. I asked Dusko Ivic if he could handle that, that they are taken to the gynaecology department in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this aside. Please answer my question. Let's see what you said to the federal police in Kiel. 1D04464 and then it is on page 041-9198 up until 9235, and there you said -- I am going to interpret it to you now. The woman reported to you personally that this rapist said to her that he would kill her if she reported him; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. It is possible that that's the way it was. But the important fact is that a rape was committed. Now, whether the rapist had threatened her, saying that he'd kill her if she reported it, that is something I can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it is the truth that matters for us, Mr. Merdzanic, not interpretations.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, rapes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said that seven women reported rape and one of these seven said that the rapist had threatened her, saying that he would kill her if she reported the rape; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can no longer remember whether it was exactly that way, maybe yes, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4 in this document. Page 4. Now let's see. Paragraph 6, paragraph 6 from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] [As read] "I must add, however, that the seven women who had been examined in Prijedor, and about whose situation evidence had been produced, were sought out in the camp by their tormentors on the following day." [Interpretation] Let's see where you said: [In English] "... I do not want to even imagine what the soldiers would have done to the women if they had found them because one woman told me in our conversation at the clinic that the soldier who raped her threatened to murder her if she reported what had happened." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here precisely. I gave my statement to the international court, describing these rapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about this paragraph. I'm asking you about this fact. Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is contained in those papers from Kiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that some tank operators outside the camp quarrelled with Major Kuruzovic because he allowed to have these women examined?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We found out only later that these were tank operators because they came to the Trnopolje camp with two tanks and they quarrelled with Major Kuruzovic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D04458, that's what you stated in the Brdjanin case on page 11819. I'm saying this for the benefit of the participants here so that they could follow what we're discussing. Did you state once that a soldier was detained because he was drunk and he drove a tank -- I see. A soldier was detained and the tank operators came to the entrance of the barracks and they asked for him to be released.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put it differently. I said that to the best of our knowledge, these tank operators who came to Trnopolje went to the military barracks and one of their soldiers had been detained there on account of that and they asked for him to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was detained because of rape; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard, because of that rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time was up some minutes ago, but how much longer do you need? I take it that you -- it's time for you to wrap-up your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best, Excellency. I need about ten minutes or so to deal with certain questions because every sentence needs to be challenged and double-checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to repeat that sentence, but I'll allow you to continue or conclude in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I'm not going to deal with the things that have already been admitted. In your interview with the OTP, I see that it's somewhere in Stakic, you said that you never saw a politician come to Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an inmate, like others, and politicians did not report to me. I know that on one occasion a delegation came. I think they were military people, though. I do not remember any politicians coming. Now, whether they actually did come or not, that is something I cannot confirm or deny with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that people could be allowed to go home if a Serb friend would offer guarantees for them; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After journalists discovered the camp and when the International Red Cross visit was announced, then the Serbs allowed people who had a place to go back to leave the camp. If someone also provided guarantees for them. Even this man Cedo who worked at the heating plant asked for me and they refused and they said that he shouldn't even ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of May when the Red Cross came -- actually, how often did they come, the Serb Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came every day, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The trouble that these seven women experienced, was this reported to the Serbian Red Cross or only to Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was reported through Dusko Ivic and the Red Cross, and it's only then that they talked to Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for Karlovac, the -- it was the UNHCR and the International Red Cross that were in charge of that convoy; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you leave as part of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left in that last convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now, since I don't have enough time, I'll see if there's any time left actually. I'm not going to mention the country that you live in. I'm just going to ask you the following. Within the agreement you reached with the OTP, did you ask for assistance several times, meaning that you did not want to be repatriated back to Bosnia, you wanted to stay in the country that you were in?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is not something that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D4853, and could it not be broadcast. Please take a look at this. In the first paragraph it says that the country, or rather, the embassy of that country agreed to grant exemption from repatriation to the individuals that the Tribunal needs as witnesses; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never asked for that and I never had any problem to stay on where I was. Maybe it went through the Tribunal, but I can no longer remember really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is your name not referred to here as well as the members of your entire family?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I really do not remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you can see that Deputy Prosecutor Blewitt wrote and requested this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it must have been between the OTP and the authorities of the country where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who gave them the names of your family?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you only discuss it verbally or did you write something to Mr. Gladstone? Because this is a request made by the investigating team. Did you communicate with the OTP in writing or only verbally?

utterances.text: Are you saying here under oath that this Office of the Prosecutor was working without any -- without informing you of anything, you didn't know about it, without any initiative from your side?

utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin your evidence, we have some administrative matters. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to make a motion to exclude portions of Mr. Brown's report. I don't see any harm in him being here for that and I think I can just go ahead. And I understand that it could possibly be argued that this is evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct under Rule 93(A) and it's our position that in -- that rule requires that the evidence be in the interests of justice before being admitted. And given the scope of this trial, combined with the lack of resources for the Defence, we don't believe that it would be in the interests of justice to widen the scope of the trial any further than it's already been widened. So for those reasons we ask that you exclude the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before I start could I just say we are assisted today on the Prosecution side by Ms. Sarah Raveling. Your Honours, I can respond to that. And I thank Mr. Robinson for sending the e-mail giving us notice that he was going to raise this issue. I notice that what he didn't argue to Your Honours is that the material in these sections was not relevant, that is because it is relevant and when these issues have come up in the past that's the test Your Honours have applied. You have found at -- that these types of evidence are admissible, even if not specifically listed in the indictment, general elements of crimes against humanity, that was at T-5480 on 19 July 2010. Elements of underlying offences, same cite. Command and control, same cite, in relation to General Rose where we were talking about events in Gorazde and Bihac. Similarly, effective control, the same cite, and intent as well as pattern and JCE. Previously Mr. Robinson on 9 June 2011 at T-14511 to -12 conceded that similar evidence in relation to expert witness Dorothea Hanson was admissible because it was relevant and put issues in context. And I think if you look at Mr. Brown's report, the report itself explains why this material is included and why it's relevant and important. That's on page 17, paragraph 1.19, the very first sentence of the first part that the Defence would like to exclude. Mr. Brown explains: "Although this report is directed primarily towards the activity of the 5th Corps/1st Krajina Corps in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is important to note that events in Western Slavonia impacted on or were related to subsequent events in the Bosanska Krajina." And goes on to speak about how this section of the report is relevant to the 5th Corps - later 1KK's - command staff and unit experiences and the features of these operations in Western Slavonia were later observed in the Krajina, the area directly linked to this part of this indictment. And he explains that this included co-operation with local TO units, arming of the Serb population, et cetera. In the second section regarding Jajce and Operation Vrbas that the Defence seeks to exclude, if you were to look at page 144 of the report, paragraph 2.222, I won't read it all, but similarly, the report itself contains an explanation of why this evidence is significant, showing how at this time-period and very quickly the 1KK, 1st Krajina Corps, were in a position to plan, launch, and command large-scale military operations under difficult circumstances and execute and take direction of the Main Staff and that the Main Staff would have knowledge, involvement, and direct these operations. So this material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 5th Krajina Corps or 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 5th Corps -- sorry, it's 1st Krajina Corps in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to Vrbas?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 5th Corps? But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if you see what -- if you look at paragraph 2.222 of the report, which is on page 144 - I'll make sure I've got my cite correct - it's speaking of the 1st Krajina Corps's ability in that section. So my submission is that this material is relevant, it's an expert report, and of course experts are allowed to draw on a wide range of sources in their material to reach their conclusions. I don't think you can dice up an expert report the way arguably you may be able to with a fact witness about what's relevant. And finally, that there is no prejudice whatsoever in this material being included because the issue now shouldn't be one of admissibility, but later the Court will be able to assign the correct weight, if any, to these sections. And it may be helpful to understanding the report as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from the issue of relevance in terms of pattern or similar thing, can I ask you, Mr. Nicholls, whether Prosecution should be able to show such an example using an example of an operation that is included in the indictment at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not sure exactly what you're asking me. It's my fault, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- personally, speaking for myself, I don't see why the -- such circumstances should be shown using an example of an operation that is not in the indictment. Put otherwise, the Prosecution should be able to use evidence relating to operation of the 1KK covered in the indictment, to show that it was able to launch such operations and to show that the Main Staff was closely involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct, Your Honour. And I think that's right and Operation Corridor features, for example, heavily in the report. But my understanding of why these sections are included in the expert report, which was written quite some time ago, I believe that at the time it was written and admitted in the Brdjanin case, for example, those were not parts of the indictment. However, the -- Mr. Brown, from my reading of the report, found that these operations were useful and necessary to understanding the way that the 1 Krajina Corps operated and do show the pattern of their ability to conduct these type of operations and the connection to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And with respect to the first issue, the events in Croatia, did the Chamber not issue a decision ruling that those events are not relevant or necessary for this case? I remember that a couple -- in a couple of decisions such a ruling was made, in particular in Babic decision, 92 quater and the adjudicated facts. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I can be of assistance because I have been in court or led witnesses on occasions when that issue has come up. I think that can be -- I think it was understood, both by the Court and by the parties, as being dependent on the particular context. You -- I think the Court correctly recalls the Babic ruling, on the other hand, as Mr. Nicholls has indicated, there have been witnesses through whom evidence about Croatia was led and clearly deemed relevant and, indeed, the accused has raised issues related to Croatia in his cross-examinations. So I think it -- as we've progressed throughout the case, that determination has been dependent upon the particular issue involved. I mean, we've heard evidence, for example, with respect to any number of steps that were taken along the way toward the identification of ethnic entities, the declaration of regions of autonomy of a state, the extent to which we were echoed in Croatia by witnesses who -- from whom that evidence was elicited in both direct and cross-examination and clearly deemed relevant by the Court. So sorry for a long answer, but I think while the Court correctly recalls the Babic ruling, the application of that issue -- of that guide-line has clearly been dependent upon the individual circumstances and the extent to which it may offer genuine assistance to illuminating the issues before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't have time to go through all the transcript you cited now, but were they not related to Sarajevo events, sniping and shelling, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours, but also to Gorazde, which was part of the basis that those events were not in the -- were not in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I also recall for you another ruling that you made relating to the municipalities portion of the case and Brcko, when you actually ruled that crimes that had been in the indictment as scheduled incidents which were stricken under Rule 73(D), that evidence could not be led because there was already sufficient evidence in the municipalities of a pattern. And I think that this is the same situation. It's even -- Rule 73(D) wouldn't have any force to it if the Chamber could strike out things and yet have things that don't even appear in the indictment become part of the evidence unless there's a good necessity for it. And if I can just take a moment to make a small reply to what's been said by the Prosecution. They've told us that the evidence is relevant and I don't doubt that for a minute. For Western Slavonia they want to show that they were arming the population, that they were co-operating with paramilitaries, that they were providing propaganda about genocide against Serbs, all of which was also done in Bosnia. And so it's relevant, but is it necessary? And your decision that you make today with this witness is going to also have an impact on what evidence you'll hear in the Defence case. Because once you start hearing evidence about Western Slavonia, you can be sure that we will rebut that evidence with witnesses. And therefore, the impact on the trial for admitting evidence not charged in the indictment will go beyond the few paragraphs of this report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a look again at Gorazde situation, but with respect to Sarajevo sniping and shelling, I think I made it clear that, while it is not very helpful, but the Chamber did not find it appropriate to exclude that part -- and then I advised the Prosecution to concentrate on the indictment issues -- issues included in the indictment. Yes -- I remember, Mr. Tieger, you rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Just a quick note about the -- what I would say is the false analogy to 73 bis. Two quite different things. On the one hand in the 73 bis circumstance, the Prosecution tells the Court it won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say I believe you're correct, Your Honour, about the incidents, but there is just a difference between the general pattern which the expert draws upon for his report and specific schedules -- incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a break now for half an hour and resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I neglected to introduce our legal intern who's here for -- her name is Magdalena Eaton and I would like to recognise her now before you break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
