utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to grant the accused's request to exclude paragraphs 1.19 to 1.28 and 2.219 to 2.222 of Ewan Brown's expert report. With respect to paragraph 1.19 to 1.28, the Chamber considers that they concern the activities of the 5th Corps in Croatia. The Chamber recalls its previous rulings, that evidence dealing with military campaigns in Croatia is not relevant to the indictment in this case. Here I refer to paragraph 27 of this Chamber's decision on second Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts issued on 9th of October, 2009, as well as paragraphs 16 to 21 of the Babic 92 quater decision of 13th of April, 2010. As for paragraph 2.219 to 2.222, the Chamber notes that they deal with the Operation Vrbas conducted by the 1st Krajina Corps in the Jajce municipality, which is not listed in the indictment. While the Prosecution submits that this is relevant in order to show the way in which the 1st Krajina Corps operated in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Chamber considers that this can be shown through evidence on operations in areas covered by the indictment. In this regard, the Chamber notes that Ewan Brown's expert report includes material related to other operations directly relevant to the indictment. Therefore, given the size and the scope of this case, there's no reason to include this material, which is clearly outside the scope of the indictment. The Chamber disagrees with the Prosecution's submission that excluding passages of an expert report is not feasible in the same way as excluding evidence of a fact witness would be. If anything, it is quite the opposite. Given the expertise of this witness in this area, the evidence he gives should be focused as much as possible on matters that are directly relevant to the indictment. An expert witness differs from a non-expert witness. Accordingly, the Chamber once again encourages the Prosecution to limit its evidence on matters relevant to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to municipalities directly covered by the indictment. That's the ruling. Let the witness take the solemn declaration. Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to do quickly now is just go very quickly through your background and the way that the report came into existence in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have, please, and it should not be broadcast, 65 ter 11118, which is Mr. Brown's CV. And while that's coming up, Your Honours, if I could just say that we will introduce or seek to tender a redacted CV as well. The CV has always been under seal in previous cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just very quickly, Mr. Brown, this is an updated CV; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I just want to focus on section (b) for our purposes now. As we see here, you joined the OTP as an analyst in 1998. In 2000 you were promoted to a senior analyst position. And in 2004 until you -- you became the MAT team leader, the military analysis team; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it was during that employment here that you wrote the report we're going to discuss today?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it, provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3912 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe I can bring up now 65 ter 11118A, the redacted version should be available. And we could tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3913, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now just to bring up on the screen could we please have 65 ter 11117, a report entitled "Military Developments in the Bosanska Krajina, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Brown, very briefly, it's spelled out actually in the report, but if you could just tell us, generally, what was the aim of this report? What were you trying to achieve with putting this report together?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: When I first arrived at the OTP in 1998, I was made aware of a document collection that had been seized in Banja Luka, which was the archive of -- part of the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps. I was at that time tasked to support a number of cases, and that collection came to my notice. Although it had been used in part, it hadn't, I believe, been systematically reviewed. I asked my line manager if I could undertake the task of systematically reviewing that collection, in part to help me understand, support the cases I was tasked with and also to support my knowledge of the military activities in the Krajina area, which was one of the areas I was asked to look at. My manager agreed that I could start reviewing this material, which I did. And it became clear to me that I thought it was a very valuable archive and I started bringing -- I started making notes myself initially actually on what I was finding in the collection and brought that to the attention of Ms. Korner, Ms. Joanna Korner, who was then one of the senior attorneys on the Brdjanin/Talic case. She suggested that I write a report in relation to what I was finding from this material. And that was agreed with my line manager at the time was the leader of the military analysis team. But in essence the outline of the report is provided in the introduction which was to provide a background analysis for that team at the time on the activities of the JNA and the VRS operating in the Krajina area in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, briefly, it is contained -- but what are -- what were the main sources for the report? What categories of sources did you use?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The report is predominantly sourced from contemporaneous documents from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps. There are a number of additional documents, smaller in number, police documents, some political minutes, and a small number of open-source material, maybe one or two video -- video-clips as well. But it's overwhelmingly documents from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell us what, in your view, you might consider limitations of the report or the parameters of the report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Your Honours, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that there are limitations in the report itself. There are temporal limitations. This document really only deals predominantly with 1992. There are some references to 1991. There are some references to documents in 1993 that reflect back to 1992, but it's predominantly relating to 1992 in time. As I said the sources are predominantly from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps, which I think is a very valuable collection and it is backed up by documents that, I think, assist the understanding of that collection, but there is a limitation in that it is predominantly based on that archive. It's also not a report that discusses every feature of activity in the Krajina area. I think I would probably still be writing that today if I had to. So there is a selection to some extent, a narrowing, based on what I was finding in the archive. And it isn't -- a background study or at least it was initially written as a background study and it isn't on every single issue in the Krajina in 1992. So those are some of the -- some of the limitations, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've prepared a couple of errata sheets for this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 11103.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very simply, that is one of the first errata sheets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, please, 23515.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that a more recent errata sheet from your review, again, of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the report, 11117, and the two errata sheets that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will all be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P3914 through 3916 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the background. Now we will begin talking about the substance of the report. I want to ask you first about some early military developments which you discuss in the beginning of the report. For everybody, the questions I'm going to go into now are found on the executive summary on page 5 and concern, Mr. Brown, what you've described there as a twin-track policy adopted by the JNA in the early months of 1992 to reduce tensions and yet the provision of aid and arms to Bosnian Serbs and then, in your words, a growing convergence between the JNA and the SDS. And then I will also touch briefly on the 16th Assembly Session strategic objectives. And here, just for the record, we are beginning to go into pages 12 to 24 of the report. Could I please have the first exhibit, the first document I want to show, that's 65 ter 01872, a 2nd Military District report dated 20th of March, 1992. You actually footnote this right at the beginning of your report, footnotes 2 and 5, and could you just tell us why you selected this -- this document for your report and also why you thought it would be relevant to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think when I looked at some of the early 1992 documents, the JNA -- the 5th Corps documents, this twin-track policy seemed evident. On the one hand there were a number of references, in fact quite a few from the 5th Corps in their regular combat reports, indicating that the situation in Bosnia was beginning to deteriorate. The 5th Corps at that time was predominantly operating in Western Slavonia, although it had got forces still in Bosnia. And in their daily combat reports there were a number of references to ethnic tensions, divisions, and some references in their own reports that they were trying to take measures to defuse some of those tensions. However, as the months went on in 1992, especially in and around March and April time, it seemed to me that, on the one hand, they were still reporting ethnic divisions but that there were a number of references indicating that they were supporting and certainly affiliated and siding with the position of the Bosnian Serbs and, in some cases, direct references to the SDS. This document is a document written by the commander of the 2nd Military District, the 2nd -- the JNA 2nd Military District which was headquartered then in Sarajevo, and it's written quite late in terms of right at the, if you like, the beginning of the real difficult period of April. And it's a summary by General Kukanjac, who was the commander of the 2nd Military District on what he believed the situation in Bosnia -- what was happening in Bosnia and it is being sent to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, in essence the senior JNA headquarters in Belgrade. And it summarises on the one hand that there's growing ethnic difficulties in Bosnia, but it also seems to show that Kukanjac and the 2nd Military District certainly believe that the position of the Bosnian Serbs is more justified and it references the issue of volunteers, that is, individuals outside the JNA, and that they are being provided arms and weapons. It also makes reference, in the latter part of the document, of their concern that TO weapons were going to -- were insecure and that they wanted to take control of those weapons. The Territorial Defence was actually a republican asset, if you like, not a JNA asset, and at least technically, I guess, the weapons were under the control of the Bosnian government. But it seems evident that the JNA are worried that some of those weapons are going to be out of their control and they are taking measures or suggest measures to take some of these TO weapons under their control. So those are some of the key themes I think that come out of this document written on the 20th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3917, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now and ask you some questions about developments the next month. We were just looking at 20th of May -- 20th of March. Moving on now ahead to May, skipping April, and ask you about some entries in the Mladic notebooks which were not available to you at the time you wrote your report, but which you later had the opportunity to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if I could now go to P01477 and page 255 in the English. It should be page 262 in the original if we need to show the original as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, again, what we're going to look at is General Mladic's notebook entries from the 6th of May, 1992, prior to the creation of the VRS. So, again, if we can go to 255 of the English. All right. And there we see that the entry is the 6th of May, 1992. If we can go to the next page. And I'm concentrating now, Mr. Brown, the second half of the page "talks," beginning at 1920 between General Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Adzic, and others. And I'd ask you to comment on this entry and what we see happening now in early May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe if I step back a couple of days before this. The situation of the JNA was, at least officially, made slightly more difficult by the pronouncement of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which happened, I believe, on the 28th of April which made the position of the JNA in Bosnia somewhat, at least officially, difficult in that the FRY was only going to consist of Serbia and Montenegro. Not long after that declaration, I believe within a day or two, General Adzic, who was Federal Secretary for National Defence, a senior JNA officer, visited Bosnia and did a tour. There was a reference in a 5th Corps document that his visit -- he came to Banja Luka and probably briefed some of the general -- some of the staff there about what was going to happen to the JNA in Bosnia. Concurrently with this, General Mladic became, at first, deputy commander of the 2nd Military District and then commander of the 2nd Military District. And this meeting comes on the 6th of May, so a few days after this activity has occurred. And it seems to me that this is a key meeting - there may have been others - but this is a key meeting in relation to the transformation of the JNA forces remaining in Bosnia, as well as an articulation from the SDS leadership about where the new Bosnian state was to be -- the footprint of that state. And it's of note that General Adzic is also involved in these discussions. And may be if I go through some of the key issues from this meeting that I think could be of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is what I was going to ask you next, Mr. Brown. If you could just draw our attention to the parts you find significant. I think we can move to the next page, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Maybe before we go to that page, the first bit identifies what's called problems. I don't know if that's problems that General Mladic has highlighted or if it's general problems that the whole group are discussing. Problem G states - this is on page 256: "If we opt for the war option we must clearly find the objectives of the war and relations with the enemy and our allies." And then there are references in the diary that Mr. Karadzic then speaks and some of the points noted down by Mladic on page 257: "We will soon be one state and one army. "We are controlling the Serbian settlements in the city and expanding them." I would assume that that probably relates to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'd like to make an objection to this. This is -- I'm objecting on the grounds that this is outside of the scope of this witness's expertise, to be interpreting a meeting about general goals of the Bosnian Serbs. He's here to give evidence, very limited to the Krajina and its military situation there. Secondly, an expert witness is not allowed to give any opinions on the acts, conduct, or mental state of the accused. And so we're -- now he's giving his opinion on a meeting in which General Mladic and also Dr. Karadzic are present. And I don't believe that he should be allowed to give his opinion or interpretation on anything about that meeting that relates to the acts, conduct, or mental state of Dr. Karadzic. So I think that this type of testimony is, number one, outside the scope of the witness's expertise; and number two, it touches on the acts and conduct of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's absolutely not outside the scope of the report. It's within the temporal time-frame of the report. It's about a meeting between the person who would become the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and the commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska. The witness is an expert witness who has identified -- who's analysed, excuse me, virtually all of the 1st Krajina Corps documents. It's also apparent from his report that -- and is included in his report and is part and parcel of it, the analysis of the way that the goals, objectives, and tasks from the political leadership were submitted to the Main Staff of the VRS and then became military operations on the ground in order to achieve those goals as occurs in the state of war in any country. So it is not speculation, I would say, for the witness to analyse a meeting between these two very important leaders of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. And he is -- the witness is an expert who is able to draw conclusions, and I think it would be extremely strange for a military expert whose report concerns, in part, the strategic goals, the 16th Assembly Session, to not be able to talk about meetings between the key players at that session that occurred that month six days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, if I could reply that, if this is so important to the Prosecution, it should have been in his report and it should have been -- or an addendum to his report. And they are now expanding the scope of his testimony and, I say, going beyond the expertise. This is a person who studied the 1st Krajina Corps, their collection of documents, and their operations. And now he's giving evidence, or purporting to give evidence, on broader areas for which we contend we've not been notified and he's not qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if I can just respond to that, Your Honour. First, I'm not aware on any prohibitions on an expert giving opinions on the acts or conducts of the accused, as Mr. Brown is in this context. Second, it is not outside the report. This is foundation to the 16th Assembly Session, the strategic goals, which are, we will see, discussed in this period before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you in terms of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is plenty -- there is notice, Your Honours because, one, all of these entries were notified that they would be used in the testimony; two, Mr. Brown did a report after his review of the Mladic notebooks, which was disclosed to Defence and Defence and included this entry. So there is notice that these topics would be covered. It's the same topic as what's included in the report. And third, there is no way that he could have analysed this material in 2002 because it had not yet been seized from General Mladic's family's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just make one point. The short report that was a review of the Mladic diaries was disclosed on the 22nd of December, 2010, so almost one year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, now, Mr. Nicholls said that he was not aware of any prohibition on the expert giving opinion evidence on acts or conduct of the accused. Can you assist us with the authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'm just looking for that right now and I can -- it's going to take me about five minutes, but I know there is authority on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may, what I think what Mr. Robinson may be getting at is an expert can't testify to the ultimate issue his opinion in the guilt or innocence of the accused, but of course an expert can testify to the acts or conduct of the accused. Every accused who testifies -- who is put on trial in this courtroom, if an expert is called, if it's going to be relevant, it's going to, in some way and in very often direct ways, speak about what that accused did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can start to give you some authority now for this. First is the Appeals Chamber decision in the ICTR, in Nahimana versus Prosecutor in the judgement at paragraph 212 and the Appeals Chamber decision in the Renzaho versus Prosecutor case, the judgement of the 1st of April, 2011, at paragraph 288 and these decisions say that "An expert witness cannot, in principle, testify himself or herself on the acts and conduct of the accused persons without having been called to testify also as a factual witness." And then there's some cases for the ICTR in the Trial Chamber level. Prosecutor versus Nizeyimana, further decision on the admission of evidence of Dr. Alison Des Forges of the 15th of March, 2011 at paragraph 11, which says that an expert witness may not testify on the acts and conduct of the accused and the admission of her -- those portions of her report were redacted. And then the Appeals Chamber has also said that the expert witness cannot testify about the criminal responsibility of the accused, which includes his mental state. So those are some of the citations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here the -- General Mladic's diaries has been already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, and we don't have any objection to him reading any portions of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As an expert, is he not able to give his opinion as to the events that would lead to the formation or establishment of an army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he -- it's probably within his expertise to give evidence how the 1st Krajina Corps was formed, but not -- I wouldn't say that the formation of the VRS, for example, would be within his expertise or even, certainly, the political deliberations which led to that. I think there was also a case -- maybe you know more about this than I do -- I'm sure you do, but in the Popovic case, wasn't there an issue about General Rupert Submit's expertise to testify about the VRS and it was -- he was not allowed, as I recall - I might be wrong about this - but I'm recalling that he wasn't allowed to testify as an expert about the operation of the VRS because his expertise, while significant as a military officer, wasn't in that particular -- studying that particular army. So I think that just because someone's a military expert doesn't give them carte blanche to testify about military issues in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, briefly, Your Honours, one, if we look at the Popovic case -- I don't have the cases cited at hand that Mr. Robinson has cited. However, we can see from the Popovic case those -- that is not the practice in this Tribunal and do not control -- Mr. Butler, just, for example, testified at length, as he has in many trials here about events in Srebrenica and including in that the activities, conduct, of the accused in those cases and that has never been seen in any way improper. Second, this is very late, to now be saying while the expert is on the stand that he doesn't have expertise in this issue. We notified the Defence, as we must, with our 94 bis notification back in 2009 that Mr. Brown would be an expert. They had the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. Robinson's objection is that while Mr. Brown is qualified as an expert in relation to the VRS military operation in the Krajina region, but not in relation to the Main Staff itself. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you on -- in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What Mr. Robinson is now challenging are aspects of the report which focus heavily on the relationship of the Main Staff to the 1KK, the six strategic objectives and the way the political goals were translated into military operations. That is all extremely clear from the report that was disclosed under 94 bis, triggering his 30-day response. When they did respond to the report, which they did not, except for asking Mr. Brown to cross, on 11 May 2009 the Defence wrote, paragraph 33: "He does not challenge the fact that the witness is an expert and that his report is relevant." So if at that time there were portions of the report in which there was not expertise, the challenge should have been made then, but I think the report and Mr. Brown's background shows that he is, in fact, an expert in these areas. He's been qualified multiple times in the Brdjanin case, Krajisnik case, which was a similar political leadership case. He testified an expert in that case on the basis of the same report, slightly different version but the same report, to the same issues. So there's precedent that he has been qualified and is an expert on these areas. The 1KK and the military operations of the 1KK can't be hermetically sealed from the events in the time that are the subject of his report. The report talks about how the strategic objectives were announced at the 16th Assembly Session, for example, one of those was the corridor operation. Within days the corridor operation is launched by General Mladic, issuing directives to General Talic. That is an integral part of the report and his, I think, expertise was manifest by the detail in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I just want to intervene on one matter that I think is very important. In our response this is exactly what we said: "He does not challenge," Dr. Karadzic, "the fact that the witness is an expert and that his report is relevant," and that's what Mr. Nicholls read out, and then there's a comma, "but reserves the right to object at trial to opinions offered outside of the expertise of the witness or to the relevance of specific testimony by the witness." I haven't seen an advocate do that too often in this courtroom to omit a section after a comma that changes the meaning and I just wanted to call that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can respond to that is because I don't see that on point. That to me is the boiler plate that if Mr. Brown starts to testify about events about the civil war in Guatemala that they reserve the right to object, not that they will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I think we have heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, I don't know if the Court wants any further explication of the case cited in response to His Honour Judge Baird's question, Nahimana. We have been looking for it. We can't find it. It is also, I would mention, another function of the belated objection. But if I can simply note this: If the Court is going to consider this matter now, looking at the portions that Mr. Robinson cited and the juxtaposition of the principle against -- the juxtaposition of the role of an expert versus the role of a fact witness this case seems to say: Look if this guy is going to testify about the underlying facts -- look, I know that this guy did something and I'm going to testify as a fact witness, then I have to be noticed as a fact witness. If that is what this case is and we haven't been able to call it up, then it is totally inapposite to the question of what an expert witness can and should be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with the Prosecution, Mr. Robinson. He -- as an expert witness, he can testify about the JNA/VRS military operations in the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1992, which should include the -- its relation with the Main Staff and also that may relate to the establishment of the VRS. And further, the Chamber notes that he's not giving his evidence as a fact witness in relation to the contents contained in Mr. -- General Mladic's diary. As such, he can give his opinion as far as he can. So objection is overruled, Mr. Robinson. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm sorry you were interrupted. If we can -- we're still on this entry for the 6th of May and you had stated that there were some points you found significant. Could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. On page 257, Your Honours, there seems to be bullet points from comments made by Mr. Karadzic and maybe continuing on with those. There's a comment: "It would be a disaster if we did not separate with them." There is a comment on: "Later, we will unite with the FRY ..." I believe that this could be a long-term aspiration, that the RS would ultimately unite with the FRY. This was a -- this was a comment that cropped up in a number of 1 Krajina Corps documents later in the war that the ultimate goal may well be, longer down the line, to unify all Serb lands. On page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I again want to -- I'm sorry if I'm -- I'm not really asking you to reconsider, but this testimony now has gone one step further to interpreting Dr. Karadzic's words and I think now that the issue is now more squarely before you with respect to the acts and conduct of the accused, I would again reiterate my objection to this witness giving any evidence concerning the acts, conduct, or mental state of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brown, where did you find the basis to come to the conclusion that ultimate goal may be longer down the line to unify all Serb lands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a section in my report in which I deal with this. If I can draw your attention to -- I'll have to go through it a little bit, sir. There are references -- I would have to go through my report, it's quite large and maybe I can do that in the break, but there are a number of references later in the war. I believe one or two after Operation Corridor is successful and later in 1992 where General Talic, in congratulating his troops, imply that the territory that they've gained and achieved there is not the -- is not necessarily the end state and that there is an objective, a potential objective, of unifying all Serb lands at some point down the line. There is also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you see that potential objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will have to go to the reference in my -- references in my report, if I can take a bit of time or maybe during the break highlight those. I believe also, and it's -- I would have to go through it again, that at the end of 1992 there's a reference in the Mladic diary a, large meeting in Belgrade sometime in December, I believe, it's not something I've looked at recently, with senior leadership figures in Belgrade in which it seems that the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership is to try and push further and faster, to consider having some unification, but at which it appears some of the Belgrade participants in that meeting are more hesitant on that. It isn't an area of my expertise, I have to say, but I do know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, until you come back with some specific bases, could you try to concentrate on your expertise, expert area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that, shall we continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we move on to page 258 of the notes, there's a reference, again attributed to Mr. Karadzic, that: "We are on the threshold of achieving our centuries' old dream of achieving creating our own state without many internal enemies." There are a number of references at the 16th Assembly Session, again, a number attributed, I believe, to -- attributed to Mr. Karadzic, about this issue of not having many internal enemies within the territory that the Bosnian Serbs wanted to control. Now, bearing in mind this meeting comes a week before the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May. Then later on on that same page it notes: "It would be good to carry out our demarcation, (a), in order for us to separate, (b) for us to form a corridor (c), for the Drina not to be a border, (d), to reach the coast." And although they're not identical to the strategic goals that were announced in the minutes of the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, it seems that what's being discussed here in this preliminary meeting relates to the objectives that were announced at the 12th of May on the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I really believe that this is going beyond the scope of this witness's expertise and touching upon acts and conduct of the accused, and I continue to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honours, it is not beyond the scope of the witness's expertise and it's quite evident from the documents. What the witness discusses in his report in large part, as I've said, is the 16th Assembly Session. The witness, when he wrote his report, did not have access to this material, which shows that a week before the 16th Assembly Session that the Bosnian Serb political leadership, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, were meeting with General Mladic and others and discussing the strategic objectives, the same tasks, the Drina not being border, number three, to reach the sea, number six. So it's not a stretch, it's not beyond his expertise in any way, I think, to be talking about the preliminary meetings that were held before the 16th Assembly, where the aspirations were discussed. It's written quite plainly in the documents. It's not beyond a military expert's expertise to talk about discussions with the military leadership which were later, very soon later, pronounced officially in the Assembly Session, spoken by Mr. Karadzic at that session. And again, I'm not aware that there is any prohibition on an expert witness talking about what an accused said at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I make just one more brief point, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wishes to have a legal debate on these -- this issue, in particular those cases cited by Mr. Robinson and their applicability to this case. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just the one point in terms of relevance and how they are -- these issues are within the expert report and are properly discussed by this witness, and that is that there have been challenges and statements that the strategic objectives are not related to military operations. And Dr. Karadzic testified in the Krajisnik case and stated that they were merely political goals that had no - I'm going off my memory - but no relation to what happened militarily following their announcement on 12 May. So it is significant within the report and we'll rebut that challenge, that these same objectives, these same tasks, are being discussed with the future military commander even before that public -- that not public, but that meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to complement that I believe the accused said in his opening that the strategic objectives were just a statement of their position vis-a-vis the European Community. I think that was at page 944 of our transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and hear from the parties on this issue and we'll continue till 1.30 and break again for half an hour and then we'll continue till 3.30. Is that agreeable to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, having had the further opportunity, albeit brief, for further research, would you like to add anything to or supplement your previous submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I -- let me just start off with my best case which is an ICTR Trial Chamber decision in the Karemera case called "Decision on Prosecution motion for reconsideration of the decision on prospective experts." And it's on the 16th of November, 2007, and I'm going to refer specifically to paragraph 21. And basically it says that: "The Chamber recalls that the established jurisprudence of this Tribunal proscribes expert evidence from usurping the function of the Trial Chamber by offering opinions that are determinative of the guilt or innocence of the accused or by averting to the acts, conduct, and mental state of the accused." And in that case the Chamber affirmed its earlier decision not to admit expert evidence. So I -- that's the best I could find to say that evidence of acts and conduct and mental state of the accused ought not to be admitted. This Tribunal has several decisions in which they say that expert witnesses should not offer his or her opinion on the criminal liability of the accused. And there's a decision in the Dragomir Milosevic case on February the 15th of 2007 and one in the Hadzihasanovic case on the 11th of February, 2004, that hold that. So what I've been able to gather is that there is a line of authority starting with that, that's -- prohibits an expert from giving their opinion on the criminal liability of the accused next to decisions like the Nahimana appeals decision, which make the distinction between an expert and a factual witness and say that experts shouldn't be giving the kind of testimony that a factual witness would be expected to give. And then, finally, to the Karemera decision that states flatly that an expert should not avert to the acts, conduct, and mental state of the accused. So I think that's the best I could tell you about the state of the law that I've been able to establish in the last 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you by any chance, Mr. Robinson, have specific circumstances or specific statements or evidence that was prohibited by the ICTR Chambers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I can do this only because I was, myself, counsel in the Karemera case. I know exactly what the statements were that were being objected to and those were interpretations by the witness, Alison Des Forges, about speeches given by the accused or statements made by them at rallies in Rwanda, which I think is pretty analogous to interpreting comments made by Dr. Karadzic at a meeting with his generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Ms. Alison Des Forges was an expert of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: She was an expert on the social and political history of Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Having looked at this quickly in the break, I think that the cases cited before the break by Mr. Robinson make clear that Mr. Brown's evidence is admissible and is exactly the type of evidence that an expert witness is expected to give. If you look at - which also concerns Alison Des Forges - the Renzaho appeals decision of 2011, there were a couple of points Mr. Robinson did not make in his initial submission. One -- the first, as he says and which we agree to, is that the expert is not called upon to testify about whether an accused is guilty and making that ultimate decision on whether the -- making that ultimate opinion on the guilt or innocence of the accused, which has not happened here or in the report. Second, if you look at paragraph 288 of that appeals decision regarding Alison Des Forges, the first part of the sentence is exactly what is happening here. "The report and testimony of an expert witness may be based on facts narrated by ordinary witnesses or facts from other evidence." And that is exactly what is happening here. He is looking at other evidence, a notebook that was not available to him. It would be the same, as it says in this appeals decision, if he looked at testimony by other witnesses. What's -- the distinction being drawn in paragraph 288 is that an expert witness -- I think the Appeals Chamber there is just talking about the difference between an expert witness and a fact witness. An expert witness cannot, suddenly without notice, without a statement, start giving factual testimony. We understand that. If Mr. Brown were to suddenly start saying that he'd met Mr. Karadzic after the war, that would be the situation being discussed there, testifying about facts outside the report. What the Appellate Chamber finds is perfectly proper and what an expert should do, is to base his report on facts stated by other witnesses or other evidence, while not directly opining or pronouncing the criminal responsibility of the accused. That's all in paragraph 2.88 [sic]. And Mr. Robinson also did not point out that in 293 of that same appellate decision regarding Alison Des Forges' historical testimony which apparently, although I don't have it in front of me, has been represented to interpreting speeches made by the accused, the Court found no error and that there was no mistake. So what Mr. Robinson's submission really is he's seized upon this one sentence in paragraph 288 and tried to broaden that to a general principle which is not included there, that an expert cannot talk about acts or conduct of an accused in any sense, where that paragraph is simply, I say, outlining the distinction between expert witnesses and fact witnesses that we all agree to. And it's -- the other decision cited by Mr. Robinson, Nahimana, paragraph 212, has exactly the same language in it, again referring to the testimony of expert Des Forges, stating that: "... while the report and testimony of an expert witness may be based on facts narrated by ordinary witnesses or facts from other evidence, a witness -- an expert witness, in principle ..." can't start suddenly veering into factual testimony. And just as an analogy, if somebody were to buy Mr. Robinson's interpretation, nobody could testify about the meaning of an intercept because he would say: No, no, he's interpreting what the accused speaking on this intercept is saying, what is happening here, it's going to the mind -- that is not the practice in this Tribunal or any other court that I know of, where an expert witness cannot talk about facts presented to him. This is a notebook, a diary, as you say has been admitted. This fact has been admitted that this meeting -- that the notebook showing this meeting taking place and what General Mladic wrote down, those facts are admitted, those facts exist, and Mr. Brown is interpreting those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson, the Chamber tends to agree with the observation of the Prosecution. Mr. Brown is not, in the view of the Chamber, going to testify as a factual evidence in relation to the events appearing in the -- General Mladic's diary. And we do not see authority, as you indicated, that the expert witness cannot comment on the acts and conduct of the accused. Further, when the witness referred to the so-called objectives or ultimate goal, then maybe longer down the line to unify all Serb lands, the Chamber does not take it that witness is testifying to the mental state of the accused; rather, given that he referred to six strategic goals and he interpreted it in his report, to which the Defence did not make any opposition -- so his response is consistent with his report. So having considered all these matters and the submission from the parties, your objection is overruled. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could now move on, please, to P01477, e-court page 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a similar topic, Mr. Brown, an entry in General Mladic's notebook for the next day. We can go over this quite quickly, I think. Can you tell us what you found significant in terms of later military developments in the Krajina, if anything, that we see from this meeting on the 7th of May, now five days before the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two things. One is that Krajisnik seems to outline the goals that were stated at the 16th Assembly Session a bit later and they seem to be a little bit more clear than the previous day's meeting, and I may be -- in relation to the 1st Krajina Corps strategic goal number one and two are of some note. The other annotation in this -- this meeting appears to be a wiring diagram or a note. It's not clear who wrote it, obviously probably Mladic wrote it, but whether it was as a result of the discussions or presentation that he himself put forward, but the wiring diagram of the outline of the army, which is on page 264 of the translation. And this seems to be what the leadership believe the structure of the army should be, and in fact, up until November 1992 that was what the VRS or the SR -- the army of the SR BiH as it was called then, the VRS, consisted of until the Drina Corps was formed later in the year. And most of the corps represented on this diagram fall from the corps that already existed in the 2nd Military District when the JNA were present. So, for example, the JNA 5th Corps became the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, but this seems to be a diagram of what they expect the army to consist of. And it was, in fact, a month or so later formally adopted as the structure of the VRS. So it would seem from these two meetings on the 6th and 7th, the military leadership and in the case of General Mladic and the Bosnian Serb leadership have got together to discuss what they believe are to be the objectives and the territory that they think they should control and discussions on the structure of the army that is to be established and was established at the 16th Assembly Session a few days after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to go through the 16th Assembly Session or pull it up on the screen. You deal with that in your report at pages 24 to 32 and paragraphs 1.38 to 1.60 and you give a summary at 1.60 of the import of the 16th Assembly Session. For the record, that is -- the 16th Assembly Session is P00956, the transcript, and P01355, the minutes. But very briefly can you just tell us what you feel from the point of view of your report and your analysis of the events in the AOR of the 1KK, what are the succinctly most important points that we see from the 16th Assembly Session?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the 16th Assembly Session, although not a stand-alone session in itself, is certainly a stand-out session. I think with the announcement of the strategic goals by Mr. Karadzic and the discussions in that Assembly session with the delegates, I would argue that it crystallises that it was the objective of the Bosnian Serb leadership to clearly announce to the delegates and to themselves that they were to -- going to be establishing their own state; that the six strategic goals, as outlined, clearly marked the territory that they believed they were going to control and that they viewed as theirs; and importantly in relation to strategic goal number one, that this territory that was marked by these goals was not going to contain a large number of individuals who they believed may be against that state and that the discussions and some of the references from the delegates would seem to indicate, in relation to that second bit, that there was -- they didn't want to have a large number of individuals who were -- they deemed as being against that state, that that would involve the resettlement, movement, or the movement out of populations within that state. I think this session is critically important too in that it establishes the army formally and it places the Presidency, president of the Presidency, in charge of the army through the Main Staff and down to the corps. So I think the session and the discussions in it, for me, stood out as giving the direction to the military about the territory that they were, in essence, to defend or take, and that in doing so, they did not want a large number of individuals who they deemed to be against that state within that state. There are other issues relating to the Assembly session, but for me those stand out. And when I say it's not a stand-alone Assembly session, I'm aware that there had already been the taking control of territory in some areas, for example, Prijedor, one of the delegates in the Assembly session discussed the activities in Krupa where, from his comments, there were no longer any Muslims there and that operation had involved elements of the JNA from the 5th Corps. I'm aware that there already had been territory, for example, in Sarajevo that had been taken under control by the Serb authorities. But for me this session, I feel, is critically important in understanding that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted their own state, that the strategic goals - in particular, number two, three, four, five, and six - articulated the boundaries of that state, and that they did not want a large number of people in that territory that they deemed to be against it; and that that would involve the resettlement of populations, including the moving in of Serbs from areas outside that footprint and, importantly, also established and placed General Mladic at the head of the Main Staff and the establishment of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, without meaning to be a pest, I really believe that that last answer, or at least part of it, infringes at least in part on the criminal liability of the accused and also goes beyond the expertise of this military expert. He's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- please continue, yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's essentially testifying that the joint criminal enterprise existed and that at this Assembly meeting at which Dr. Karadzic spoke, the participants agreed to displace the Muslim population or non-Serb population and in my opinion that, number one, is not the province of a military expert; and number two, goes directly to the criminal liability of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let me put the questions to Mr. Robinson before you respond. No, I would rather listen -- hear from you, Mr. Nicholls, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't think I should have to respond to this. I think you've made your ruling and that the ruling was clear and that from the cases we've looked at and the argument we've made that Mr. Brown's answer is squarely within his expertise and it's included in the report. He is not coming -- stating inadmissibly the guilt or innocence of the accused. He is looking at the statements, the facts of what was contained in the transcript of the 16th Assembly Session. He is looking at what happened militarily on the ground and interpreting those facts which is exactly what an expert should do and he's not straying outside the boundaries, which we've just discussed and taken a break to look up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I forgot to mention when I gave our ruling previously, but the witness clearly argued and -- that the six strategic goals were military ones and, as such, he's interpreting the items appearing in the Mladic diary or in the 16th Session of the Assembly as an expert. He's not giving -- the Chamber does not think he's giving evidence as to the guilt of the accused or the joint criminal enterprise or something like that. I will allow the evidence to continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I have P03590.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, we're now two days after the 16th Assembly Session, 14 May 1992. This is a document from your report concerning a meeting held in Kljuc. And could you just tell us why you selected this document and what you find significant about it. And while you're doing that, could you just tell us who Branko Basara is and what his involvement was, if any, before this meeting in military operations in what would become the 1KK area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Branko Basara, Your Honours, was a former JNA officer who became a brigade commander of the 6th Brigade. He had fought in Western Slavonia and was sent back from Western Slavonia, I believe in April 1992, to the area of Sanski Most. He is present, I believe, at this meeting because it's signed and drafted by -- or at least the 30th -- sorry, the 30th Partisan Division, the 30th Division, was a subordinate of the 1st Krajina Corps. So you had the 1st Krajina Corps. Below that you had the 30th Division and below that you had a number of brigades and one of those brigades was the 6th Brigade and that was the brigade that was based in Sanski Most. Prior to this meeting on the 14th of May, part of that brigade had been involved in operations in Bosanska Krupa. So when one of the delegates at the 16th Assembly Session had mentioned that there were no longer any Muslims in Krupa, that they had all gone over the river, part of that brigade had been involved in the actions in the preceding period. But the reason I believe he's at this meeting is because the 30th Division, its area of responsibility covered a number of municipalities rather than just one. So whereas the 6th Brigade predominantly dealt with Sanski Most, although it did operate in Krupa and it did operate in Kljuc, I believe, as well, the 30th Division covered a number of municipalities. So this meeting appears to be a joint civil/military meeting with the senior military figure of that area, which was Colonel Stanislav Galic, who was the commander of the 30th Division; a number of other military officers, including Branko Basara who was one of his subordinate brigade commanders; and the municipal heads of the municipalities that the 30th Division covered. And it comes two days after the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we could just go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, when you testify that part of that brigade, i.e., the 6th Partisan Brigade had been involved in the actions in the preceding period, I take it that you came to that conclusion having read documents to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not as a factual witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there's a reference in my report to a -- I think there might even be two references, but there's a report -- a war bulletin of the 6th Brigade and I believe there might -- there's a partial diary of that brigade, highlighting that they -- some of the places they'd been involved in and Krupa is one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is such-and-such document exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And maybe I'll bring that document up in a little while.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could just quickly go to page 3 of the English and B/C/S. We appear -- we see there a briefing of the meeting in Banja Luka, as it's described, and the six strategic goals were presented. Can you just tell us what to you that signifies?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to me that they're passing down the goals down the chain down at the municipal level. There's a comment that may have some interest where it says: "It was assessed -- it was assessed that this army can occupy a large territory but this is not necessary because it would be impossible to defend in the following period ..." There were some comments, I believe, at the 16th Assembly Session when some of the delegates were saying we should be taking this territory and that territory and there were some discussions that, in essence, they shouldn't bite off more than they can chew; in essence, they shouldn't take more than they can hold. So whether this is a reflection of the comments -- some of the comments that were made at the 16th Assembly Session, it is possible. But it would seem to me that what they're doing at this joint military/civilian meeting two days after the Banja Luka Assembly Session that those strategic goals are being disseminated again and they're being reinforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know if I should also point out on page 4, there's a bullet that says: "Implement the decision from the meeting in Banja Luka but submit them to the commands of units and municipalities ..." I don't know if that's a typo but, again, whether this would seem to indicate that the meeting in Banja Luka was not some irrelevant discussion and that the discussions in relation to the goals, the setting up of the army, the integrating of the TO, that those decisions should be implemented down the chain at the municipal level. It also says: "All forces of the SR BiH of Bosnia-Herzegovina should work towards the same goals ... war profiteering should be prevented." And also there should be meetings held every 15 days. So this group presumably want to make sure that they are informed about what's going on. The first part of the meeting is a briefing from each municipality, maybe going back to Your Honour's point about the 6th Brigade, I think in relation to the point in Kljuc on page 2, there is a reference that part of the 6th Brigade is already -- has already been involved -- it says: "At the time of the take-over of power, units from the 9th Corps and the 5th Corps (a battalion of the 6th Brigade) were securing Kljuc ..." So I don't know if that helps your question earlier, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown. If I could just direct you to footnote 132 of your report, is that the document you were referring to? This is on page 40 of your report. And maybe we could bring that up. I believe it's 00891.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, I think that was the reference I was reaching for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 00891, please. And perhaps go to the next page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If we look down there, several paragraphs down: "Under the command of Colonel Branko Basara, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade took part in the following campaigns ..." Amongst others, we see there the liberation of Bosanska Krupa and then we talk about later events. Just to be clear, is that the reference you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I tender that then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, continuing on about these early developments but switching gears a little bit, I want to talk to you now about mobilisation in this area. This would be your report, pages 37 to 39, paras 177 to 182 for the record and the mobilisation which takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I please have 65 ter 01536. While it's coming up, I'll say this is from the 20th of May, 1992, Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, "Decision on general public mobilisation of forces," signed by President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, please, what you find significant about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I really just highlighted the -- that very quickly after the Assembly session, the Presidency was issuing an instruction down through the Main Staff, down to the corps to mobilise. It had been an issue that a number of delegates at the Assembly session indicated that there should be mobilisation. And very quickly on the establishment -- or at least the formal establishment of the army, that there is a mobilisation instruction coming down from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3919.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I Could have 65 ter 20344 on the screen. This is a 1KK command document from the next day, the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You cited this various times in your report. And could you just tell us why you selected this document for your report, showing the mobilisation order of the 1KK on this date?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There's a number of issues apart from the content. In terms of timing, this is the day after the Presidency decision so it shows that the 1st Krajina Corps is following the orders and instructions of the Presidency and Main Staff. It was also a couple of days after the formal withdrawal of the JNA. I think all JNA units were meant to have left by the 19th, but in reality there was a transformation rather than a withdrawal. So it showed to me in relation to the passage of information that General Talic is responding very quickly to instructions from, in essence, his new leadership, the Presidency and also the Main Staff. In terms of the content, it makes reference to the Presidency decision in the first line. Paragraph 1, Talic instructs his subordinates to establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground. Presumably along the lines of the document we had seen on the 14th of May with Stanislav Galic having briefings and meetings with his chief. Paragraph 6 he states: "Explain to conscripts as they arrive the goals of our struggle and brief them on their duties and rights." It would seem to have echos of the goals that were discussed at the Assembly session in which General Talic, himself, was present. Paragraph 8 notes in part 4, they're to establish the closest possible co-operation with the people and legal authorities within their zones of responsibility. And paragraph 9 notes the issue that there are not to be the presence of paramilitary formations or other special organisations in the zones or his zone and the zones of responsibility of the subordinate units, but they are to be integrated into the units as volunteers. And if they refuse that, they are then to be broken up and destroyed. So it would seem to indicate that General Talic was aware that there were paramilitary groups operating potentially in his zone, but that in order to control them they were to absorb them into the army. And only if they refused that would they then be broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very quickly, Mr. Brown, to be clear for the record, you started off your answer by saying: "I think all JNA units were meant to have left by the 19th after the formal withdrawal of the JNA ..." Withdrawal from where?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Because of the new FRY, it was supposed that the JNA were meant to withdraw from Bosnia to go back to Serbia. But in reality, as we can see, certainly the 1 Krajina Corps, the 5th Corps was present, the same units were present after that withdrawal. General Talic remained in command, his staff remained in command, many of the units were the same, they maintained most of the equipment. So in terms of withdrawal, there may have been a withdrawal of Serbian officers, Montenegrin officers. But to all intents and purposes in the Krajina, the 5th Corps became the 1st Krajina Corps with all -- with much of its equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next document is from the same day, also from the 1st Krajina Corps, 04196 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification, Mr. Nicholls. Did you say withdrawal of Serbian officers? Officers from Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 04196, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While this is coming up, again it's 21st of May, 1KK command, signed by the assistant commander for morale, Milutin Vukelic, and we see that it's been -- it's handwritten that this should be sent to all units. You cite this document in quite a few places in your report. The -- this document by the morale officer of the same day is mobilisation. Can you just briefly tell us why you found this significant to include in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was a document written by a staff officer in General Talic's command, the assistant commander for morale. And in essence he produced a series of documents, certainly through 1992, which give a summary of the political circumstances and also, often, a summary of what has happened in the zone of the corps during the period -- the reporting period. And, quite often, the reports that the staff officer writes he annotates at the end that they should be disseminated to units of the corps and he uses often language like thrashed out with individual soldiers. So in essence it is a summary document about the activities above the corps in the political sphere, why they're fighting, and what's going on within their zone. And it -- the date of this document I think is important because it comes out on the day that General Talic writes his mobilisation instruction, bearing in mind that he put in his mobilisation instruction the goals and objectives - I forget the phrase - the goals of our struggle should be explained to -- as a part of the mobilisation process. It may well be that this document is part of that explanation process. And the first part of the document explains why, in essence, the 1st Krajina Corps and the Bosnian Serb army are fighting. So, for example, in paragraph 2, the document says: [As read] "Even though the oldest and constituent parts, the Serbs are exposed to unscrupulous deprivation of their rights, transformation into a national minority and genocide. In BH, the Serbian people have organised themselves politically and are firmly resolved to struggle alone to secure their historical right, national dignity and interests. The constituent Serbian people, who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population ... must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croat peoples and form their own state ... "They do not want anything that is somebody else's, anything that has not been theirs for centuries but they will not give an inch of their own territory." This issue of complete separation from the Muslim and Croat peoples would seem to echo this goal of separation that was articulated at the 16th Assembly Session. And bearing in mind, this was written by an officer who up until days before and in his career had been a JNA officer. This type of language may be of some significance. There are other references in the document that I think are of note. Paragraph 3 says: "To prevent the militant and criminal Muslim and Croatian anti-Serbian coalition and its paramilitaries from achieving their plans, the Serbs of BH are prepared and able to resist them by all means, including armed struggle." Later on they talk about that the Main Staff has been appointed, Ratko Mladic is the commander, and other elements of unified organisation in command and control have been set up. There is a reference a bit later down that page in part 2 where it says: [As read] "The army of the Serbian Republic is the army of the Serbian people of all patriots as well as of all citizens who are ready to fight in its ranks for the just goals of the Serbian people: The defence of the territorial integrity of republican peace in these areas." And for me it's as much the content as the language that this is very clearly pro-the position of the Serbs. I don't see too much tolerance in the language there. The timing is important, I think. It seems to be related to what Talic was talking about, about disseminating why they are fighting. And the last paragraph in the report indicates that: "Inform all members of the army of the contents of this report in the most suitable way." So I would believe that this report was disseminated down to the units, brigades, and divisions, and subordinate formations of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to move on now to take a look at a document that's already in evidence, the combat-readiness report, as we call it. It's D00325. And I would like to have pages 10 and 11 of the English, please, beginning with page 10. And we don't need to read through all this, but the point I want to make, Witness, is they -- in the combat-readiness report from 1993, looking back on 1992, at the bottom of page 10 and the top of page 11 there is a discussion of the two phases of the development of what is by then the VRS, called the VRS. The first phase from the 1st of April to the 15th of June, 1992, and then the second phase from June 15, 1992 to the writing of the report, which is sometime around April 1993. This report features importantly in your report, and I want to talk about these phases in somewhat reverse order, talking about the second phase first. But can you please just briefly explain from looking at this report what the two phases are about and whether this report seems accurate to you about the two phases.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is generally accurate. There might be some issues in relation to the dates because it seems to imply that the second phase where there was this more formal large-scale operations were conducted after the 15th. Well, there was some -- there was one directive which came out after the 15th. But to all intents and purposes this seems a reasonable summary of the military activity that I saw in the Krajina and elsewhere, actually, that there was this period between April and May and early June in which municipalities were taken - it says here - under the patriotic influence of the Serbian Democratic Party, using Territorial Defence units and others and that they provided, they call, protection of the Serbian people in those municipalities but they stopped at that, that they in essence secured that territory. And then there was a second phase occurring from the middle of June in which under the Main Staff and the Presidency there were, if you like, larger combat operations and more formal structured combat operations that took place. And I would seem to think that from the documentation that that is what happened. In the Krajina Corps there were municipality take-overs in May and early June, and then after that, there was a number of large military operations that the corps was ordered to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I think we're coming to the break if I have it right, but I apologise; I neglected to tender 04196, the mobilisation, the -- excuse me, the Vukelic document we just talked about.

utterances.text: We will take a break for 40 minutes and resume at ten past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could introduce the last of our interns who's present today. This is Tadej Koncar who is working with our case managers.
