utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we just left off before the break talking about the two phases of the development of the VRS, and specifically the 15th of June and that phase that started that phase being identified in the combat-readiness report. Before we move on, I just want to refer you, if I may, to on page 34, paragraph 1.69 of your report, you talk about there the issuance of orders and directions from the Main Staff down and reports coming up. And so can you just very quickly tell us what was the situation with the up-and-down chain, orders going down, decisions going down and reporting going up before the second phase, before 15 June?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think that there was -- well, there are documentary evidences that indicate that the chain of command from the Main Staff down to the Krajina Corps was operating almost instantaneously and very quickly. Not long after, for example, the mobilisation instruction on the 20th and 21 the Main Staff sent an instruction to the various corps, I believe on the 26th possibly, asking for them to supply them with information about the units of their corps and their -- the areas of operations that they were working in. And General Talic in the 1st Krajina Corps responded the following day giving that advice -- not advice but information. General Talic was sending his daily combat reports straight away to the Main Staff. There was no pause or break. The daily combat reports of the 1st Krajina Corps were usually sent twice a day. I think in 1992 there were very few days I didn't see there was two combat reports and on occasion there were also three. But I think the chain of command, bearing in mind that the 5th Corps had already been working in that area for a long time, it just seemed to be that they utilised exactly the same reporting process on the establishment with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to talk about the issuance of the first directive of June 6th and look at three documents during that period. The first is P01508, if I could have that up, please. That's a Main Staff document from 1st of June, 1992, urgent, meeting of the corps commanders, order. And could you just tell us about this document quickly in early June.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I mean, it seems clear that the Main Staff are passing on an instruction that pursuant to a Presidency decision, that there is to be a meeting in Pale on the 3rd of June and that the corps commanders are to attend, they are to brief, and to give a map indicating their corps' AOR. This may follow on potentially from the documents I just mentioned on the 26th and the 27th of May, where the Main Staff is talking about what units are in your corps and what AOR do you have and they discuss that the corps commanders to attend, to be transported by helicopter if necessary to this meeting. And it would seem to be that the Presidency is interested in this, knowing what the corps are doing and what AOR of -- what area of operations they're working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move three days past the 3rd of June to P01478, that's a Mladic notebook entry for June the 6th, a Saturday. Page 93 of the English, 92 of the B/C/S, the original I should say. This is quite a lengthy meeting and I don't want to go through the whole thing, Mr. Brown, because it will take too long. But could you just tell us the significance of this meeting, bearing in mind the meeting we've talked about from the 3rd of June and the next document we'll see, the directive, the first directive, that's issued the same day, the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think the timing is of note because a directive comes out on the same day. It seems to be a significantly detailed and large consultation involving the senior leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. Dr. Karadzic, at the beginning, notes again the SR BiH Assembly has defined the strategic aims, on page 94; reiterates the strategic objectives with comments and explanations --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just say that's on the next page of the English for Your Honours. Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: And also notes that we have to protect our territories militarily. So, again, it would seem to lend credence that the strategic goals were not just rarified statements of interest but actually had a significant meaning. The rest of the report or a lot of the report -- in fact, there are a couple of other comments from Mr. Karadzic and others. For example, on page 97 of the translation, it's noted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you find that words of Mr. Karadzic, defend militarily? I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We have to protect our territories militarily." That -- I have that on page 95 of my translation about halfway down, a little bit more than halfway down, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That would be the third page of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see -- I think actually what I see -- at the top of the page it says 94 and at the bottom of the page it says 95, but I think it's actually page 94, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's, Your Honours, just for the record, because of the numbering that is in the actual physical diary but in e-court, we are now on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit later on, page 96 or 97, I'm not sure, but Mr. Karadzic says: "The birth of a state and the creation of a border -- of borders does not occur without war ..."

utterances.text: If we do not see the passage, it's really difficult. So make sure we have the correct page, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to move a little bit slower. So we're now on the correct page, which states "96" on the top. In e-court that would be page 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then: "If we Serbs," I believe that could be a typo, "do not start thinking," rather than "to not start thinking about a state and about our territories, then we will lose." So it seems to be in this introductory part of this meeting, there is a re-emphasis on territory and a re-emphasis on strategic goals and that these goals and territories are going to be achieved militarily. The -- there is a comment on page 97 from Mr. Karadzic which seems potentially slightly ambiguous but I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could we go to page 98 of the English in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We must not put pressure to have people displaced." The remaining part of the meeting or a large part of the meeting seems to come on this page under the title where Mr. Ostojic talks and a lot of the pages after this appear, to me at least, to be the leadership discussing the detailed borders of a map. So where it goes borders and lists a large number of locations on the following three or four pages, it is possible that what is being discussed here is they have a large map and that they are plotting on that map where they believe the border of the state should be. I can't say that for sure because this doesn't involve a map, itself, but just reading the section from Mr. Ostojic, it is possible that that is what is being done. It is of note that Mr. Ostojic, when he charts that line, gets to Bratunac on page 100, notes that in Bratunac there are no Muslims in the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, that's page 101 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it may well be that he's reading on the map, plotting on the map, gets to Bratunac and puts the comment that there are no Muslims in that area and he also talks about Srebrenica, half of it being empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is completely in bad taste, trying to guess what the other person is thinking. That's one thing. Another thing is I would kindly ask for the Serbian version as well. I believe the translation may be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the other half of Dr. Karadzic's objection, which I also believe is well-founded, is: Are you comfortable that this is within the expertise of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.text: But, Mr. President, is it for a military expert to be interpreting a conversation of what people think and what they mean? I think that's going --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say another thing, Your Excellencies, because this is another thing the Prosecution is doing when they misquote. utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, when one has regard to the objection taken by Mr. Robinson, would you say that the comment of the witness was his opinion or would you say that he was speculating?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I was going to follow up on what you said. utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may just briefly, if we -- if I'm allowed to move on with my direct, we'll see that what is discussed in this meeting amongst other things are maps and the six strategic objective, one of which is the corridor, and on the same day, as Mr. Robinson thought would be proper, the directive comes out which is to seize the corridor. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, as you indicated, why don't you lead evidence you referred to first and then we come back to this issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have D00232, please. This is the directive for further actions from the Main Staff of the VRS dated 6 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly, Mr. Brown, can you tell us which, if any, parts of this directive link to military options being ordered by the Main Staff which have to do with the topics we've just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I believe they are because this directive comes out the same day as that meeting. The military directive on the 6th of June, I would argue, does three things. Firstly, or at least in summary, firstly it tasks the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to maintain a blockade of Sarajevo, and in the meeting before, I mean we didn't come to it, but it appears that part of the discussion seems to be from some of the delegates talking about the territory in and around Sarajevo that they think they should control. And that is one part of this directive. It tasks the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to maintain the blockade and to take control of certain territories in Sarajevo. Now, in relation to the 1st Krajina Corps and directly relating to strategic goal number 2, which Dr. Karadzic had announced at the 16th Assembly Session was to secure a corridor through Semberija, basically linking the 1st Krajina Corps and the East Bosna Corps. Dr. Karadzic, at the 16th Assembly Session, said that that area was of strategic importance to the Bosnian Serbs, not just because it linked the territories in Bosnia together, i.e., the Krajina and the area around East Bosna and elsewhere, but because it linked -- if they secured the corridor, it linked the territories in Krajina, in Croatia -- the Serb parts of the Krajina and also linked those two territories with Serbia. So that is why this strategic objective number two was placed so highly and so highly regarded, because it unified the Serb lands in Bosnia and also unified the Serb lands in Croatia and also with Serbia. And this directive on the 6th of June tasks the 1st Krajina Corps to conduct operations in order to secure the territory in the corridor. So when you go to the tasks of the units on -- in paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt you, that would be on page 3 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It tasks the 1st Krajina Corps and actually the East Bosna Corps to liberate territory which is in the corridor, and that is exactly what General Talic did in the proceeding weeks after this. So the directive tasks predominantly the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to do activities in Sarajevo and the 1st Krajina Corps and the East Bosna Corps to secure territory. But another area is that it continues to order the other corps, and including the 1st Krajina Corps for that matter, to maintain the lines that they've already achieved and to continue to secure their own territory. So although for the 1st Krajina Corps the focus is for the corridor, it also reminds General Talic that he has to secure the other areas within this corps. The focus for me and the importance for this document is that it links a strategic -- actually, two if you consider the Sarajevo area as well, strategic goals that were announced at the 16th Assembly Session, the goals that were discussed by General Talic in some of his orders before, the meetings that occurred in early June, this meeting on the same day, and the dispatch of this Main Staff directive for operations, which were acted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's a matter for Mr. Karadzic to take up in his cross-examination, but I wanted to find the passage but where it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may not be in this directive but it may well be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, in your testimony.

utterances.text: Your Honour, I suspect that's a reference to 83, 21 or 20 through 21, which distinguishes between -- Dr. Karadzic seems to be conflating two different things and then inventing a word that wasn't used to make this objection. But anyway, that's where one reference appears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not making anything up. In two places in the transcript the witness, I believe, said to maintain the siege of Sarajevo, which implies something that does not -- is not found in the document.

utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, no, the witness didn't use the word "siege." Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now go very quickly -- you started talking about this, Mr. Brown, P01732. 9 of June 1KK command combat report to the Main Staff signed by General Talic. And what does this tell us about the directive we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There are a number of other areas of this document that may be irrelevant, but in the last -- second-to-last paragraph, so paragraph 8 it notes that: "In accordance with the directive received" --

utterances.text: So that would be beginning on page 2 of the English, Your Honours, page 3, I believe, of the B/C/S -- page 3, I believe, of the original. utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you just tell us without going --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just kindly ask that you focus on page 82, line 18, and lines 22 and 23, as far as the blockade of Sarajevo is concerned. [In English] "To maintain blockade of Sarajevo."

utterances.text: Now --

utterances.text: We can continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, without going to all of the documents on this issue, can you tell us when did the 1KK Operation Corridor start? When did it finish, at least the first stage? And was it successful? That's a three-part, compound question, I know, but if you could -- I think it's simpler if you go through those three steps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps on the 10th of June pushed out its own order based on the directive of the 6th of June. It was a more expansive instruction, as you'd expect. There was a preliminary period between the first -- sorry, I think that period, the 10th of June, and around the 24th of June, when the corps launched Operation Corridor. There was some preliminary actions before there to secure areas that they needed to launch the operation itself. Within a very short space of time, I believe, initially they secured a very limited road on the 27th of June and a more substantive road in the first few days of July. I think it was -- it was either the 4th or 6th but I would have to check my documents. So in essence by the early part of July they had secured a corridor link to the East Bosna Corps and they spent the following few months expanding that corridor link up to the Sava River, which they achieved by, I believe, finally taking Bosanski Brod in October. It may be about the 24th of October, it may be later in the month, but around that period. So they had achieved their objective quite quickly, although it was quite a narrow corridor. And then they spent the preceding -- sorry, the following months or weeks and months expanding that corridor and it was finally secured by October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now move on to another directive, that's directive number 4. utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry about that, Your Honours. If there is an error it should be page 141 of the typed B/C/S is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But what I would like to direct you to, Mr. Brown, regarding this November 8th meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- could you wait?

utterances.text: Oh, yes. I have a hard copy, Your Honours, we could put on the ELMO if that -- if that assists.

utterances.text: I think it's coming now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, if we may what I'd like to do is go to page 146 and then 147 of the English where Mr. Krajisnik speaks, which should be the same in the Serbian language. Could you tell us what you -- what you observed in this -- at this meeting, where Mladic, Karadzic, Krajisnik are present with some of the corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This meeting seems to be similar to one that was expected in the 1st of June document we saw earlier on, where prior to the directive, the corps commanders are asked to a meeting to give their briefings on what's happening in their corps. In the first part of this meeting seem - at least from the notes - appear to be each individual corps commander giving a small speech about what's happening in their zone. And then after that there seems to be assignments -- the discussion about what should happen next. Mr. Karadzic mentions that the army has contributed enormously to the results so far, but then Mr. Krajisnik notes that there are some achievements that haven't yet been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you, sorry, and just for everybody to go to page 145 of the English so that we can see that reference to Mr. Karadzic speaking, which you just talked about. I believe it's -- that's the page you're referring to and then we'll go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if we could continue to page 146.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: On 146, Mr. Karadzic ends his section by saying: "Maybe it would be good if we solve the issue of the Drina." And then Mr. Krajisnik talks about the Drina, the Neretva. And on page 147 says: "We haven't achieved the Neretva, the sea, and the Podrinje area," those being strategic objectives announced at the Assembly session in May. "But we have achieved the corridor," objective number two; "and separation with the Muslims." He then ends this section by saying: "The most press be thing is to mop-up Orasje and then to solve the problem of the Podrinje area and the Neretva river valley as soon as possible. "The Muslims must not stay with us and they should not be given any kind of autonomy. "The most important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic - the mopping-up of the Drina. "The most important task is separation from the Muslims." Zivanovic being the Drina Corps commander. And it would seem that this is a preliminary meeting about where they had achieved their objectives to that date, but clearly that they felt that the Drina was an area that they needed to give tasks to. And that is what happened in directive four and the Drina Corps was tasked to conduct operations in the Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I won't bring it up now, but P00976 as admitted is directive four from 19 November 1992. And could I just ask, sir, do you -- just as we go along, do you recall that that was the day that directive four, the one you were just discussing, was issued?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another document now, please, that's 14815 is the 65 ter number and it's a Drina Corps command document, I'll say while it's coming up, also from the 19th of November. And it's entitled a "warning order." And it states, talking about some areas mentioned in directive four, in the first paragraph it talks about Cerska, et cetera. Can you just tell us the significance of this. What is a warning order?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Your Honours, a warning order is, in essence, a preliminary order given to military formations, notifying them of upcoming operations in order for them to prepare logistically and in other ways for that operation. It usually is followed by a more substantive order. It's in essence a preliminary order for upcoming operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we could look at page 2, please, of the English, which is still page 1 of the Serbian. And under number -- paragraphs 2 and 3, if you could just comment on what we see there, where they talk about the Zvornik Brigade under "forces" and then the tasks.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before going further. Was it supposed to give evidence in relation to events regarding Drina Corps and that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he gives evidence relating to the directives, and this is directive four. Directive four is noted in his report, although many of these documents were not available to him at the time. In July 2009 a statement, a short -- a brief statement was made --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Thank you, Excellency, but I've actually given up on objections all together and I'm not sure that the translation is right. It should read "preparatory" or something like that. I mean, really, I'm going to need a month to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may say "preparatory order," if there's a mistranslation, I don't know. But the directives are something that he does discuss and the way directives one re -- in some cases reflect the strategic objectives and the discussions of the leadership. We saw that with directive one. Directive four is similar and is cited in his report. And in July 2009 in the statement which was provided to the Defence, he went through these documents and linked them up to the conclusions he'd made in his report regarding directive one and the way that the Main Staff operated and the orders were transmitted from the Presidency to -- from the president, the Presidency, to the Main Staff and then down the chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The expertise, as far as we understand it, is the one he got through reading out all the Banja Luka document collection seized from Banja Luka. And now based upon that, he's testifying about the events relating to Drina Corps. I take it there's another expert coming in relation to that matter. Am I correct in so understanding? That's my first question. And then whether -- well, I was reluctant to put this question, but do Judges need expert's knowledge in translating directives or other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not, Your Honour. But one -- what -- the first part of your question is: Yes. The primary sources Mr. Brown used in his report were the Drina Corps documents, but he also read Main Staff documents and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not Drina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade -- that's me thinking ahead. 1st Krajina Corps documents. But he talked about the structure in the way orders were passed down in relation to the 1st Krajina Corps and what directives were and how they were used. So these Drina Corps documents from late 1992 and in early - which is the period of his report - and then early into 1993 are outside the original report, it's true, but they're on the same broader subject matter of the way the army functioned. The second part, we do have an expert who will be -- who is much more focused on the Drina Corps coming. However, in Mr. Brown's statement, which was -- as I say, was disclosed to Defence, he went through quite a few directive four-related documents and analysed them. So I think it may be useful to the Trial Chamber to see, as he's shown with directive one, that there were preparatory meetings before the directives were issued, which is the case here as well with directive four, and then that the series of orders and documents come out after the directive is issued. And the input of the political leadership in the formation of these directives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the facts, such preparatory meeting and the order was given, those facts will be established separately based upon the -- either on documents or factual witnesses? And he's linking those facts, so to speak, in terms of his interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And these -- these documents which I'm showing are -- are, in fact, the order -- the follow-up orders and some of the others which show that the -- following on from the directive, actual military operations on the ground were conducted and my impression - the witness can correct me if I'm wrong - in a parallel way to what we saw with directive one, which tends to show the way that the process worked in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just pass one observation, that is: Why couldn't the Prosecution make that exact same submission in its closing submission without this witness? All of this evidence is simply the Prosecution's closing argument in disguise from every -- this is about the sixth employee of the Office of the Prosecutor who has come and linked things together and basically put forward the Prosecution's closing argument. And you do have the discretion to determine that it's not of much assistance to the Chamber, and I would ask the Chamber to think about exercising that discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But one thing I can make sure at this moment, Mr. Robinson, is that we as Judges, professional Judges, are capable of assessing the witness -- the weight of the witness's evidence and -- so you can rest assured that this -- that the Judges are able to distinguish the submission and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that. But given the Chamber's concern with time, as constantly evidenced by the restrictions on Dr. Karadzic's cross-examination, might it not be wise, if it's the type of evidence that's not really of assistance to the Chamber, simply not to hear it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness is not here to give our closing argument. Our closing argument will be based on the evidence. The witness here is discussing military documents which he's analysed and -- and the -- and hopefully assisting the Chamber in what these documents mean in terms of what types of documents they are, the pace at which these operations take place and the documents are issued. And, yes, we will refer to these documents in our closing argument very likely. But I do object to the characterisation. The witness here is going through the documents, explaining the way directives worked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say a word? Mr. Robinson put it very mildly. I'm going to say it differently. This is an ambitious attempt, a third attempt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the Prosecution to put into evidence their indictment as an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... Mr. Karadzic, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, let's continue. But the Chamber would like you to concentrate on events that took place in the region of -- Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. All right, well in that case, Your Honours, I will, if I may, just -- I will skip through some of the documents I was going to go through that relate to directive four at this time, but try to ask the question -- the witness one more question about the directive four documentation -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can you hear me -- I don't know if -- now it's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, could I have D00325, please. That is the combat-readiness report from April 1993 looking back at 1992. And just page 160 of the document in English. I'm sorry, I don't have the reference to that page in the B/C/S, but it's right near the very end, probably the third page from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is in a section headed "Basic characteristics of the operational tactical utilisation of the Army of Republika Srpska." And I would like you to look at the top of page 160. If we could scroll up -- the other way. If you read that paragraph starting with: [As read] "Thus the primary focus of our time ..." It speaks about the corridor. It speaks about gaining control of other territory and then states: "In the last month and a half, our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje, as thereby the strategic objective of our war would be realised, one that could be defined as 'establishing contact with Serbia on the river Drina, or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier.'" So this talks about the corridor operation which is in your report and directive four which we began to discuss. Can you just explain what significance you see, if any, in this mention in the combat-readiness report looking back at 1992 and looking at where they are at the present.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to indicate that those areas, the corridor and the Podrinje, were important. I think it -- those areas were reflected in operational directive four, which was a document that was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps and it was in the Krajina Corps archive. I think from the other documents I reviewed, subsequent to the writing of this report, there seems to be a clear chain that flows from the senior leadership down through the directives for operations in those areas, including the corridor, including the Podrinje area, and that subordinate formations in the Drina Corps carried out operations as they were requested. Whether they had the success, that's for somebody else to deal with. But the Drina Corps documents and operational directive four seemed to me to reflect very much the directive one and, actually, directive three, which was also pushed out in August dealing with slightly different issues. And for me they relate back to the strategic goals that were articulated in May and, in fact, on the preceding page to this, there is a reference to that, that the strategic goals were defined and formed the basis on which the Main Staff and subordinate units, guide-lines they called them, conducted operations. And I think strategic directive number four was very similar to directive number one. It was a slightly more polished document, I think, slightly more detailed. But the Drina Corps took the tasks, as all the other corps, and certainly the 1st Krajina Corps did, took the tasks that were sent to them in that directive and there were other documents from the Drina Corps, and subordinate formations of the Drina Corps that would seem to indicate that they did what was asked of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we please go back one page, 159, for Your Honours to see and for my colleagues to see the section that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you point out the section you were talking about, Mr. Brown, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it's in that second paragraph. [As read] "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the Army of the RS, the commands and units, served as a general guide-line upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles. This means that objectives were set before us rather than specific tasks spelled out, although the President of the Republic, as the supreme commander of the armed forces ... did orally assign a number of tasks which were of general and vital significance to our struggle in protecting the Serbian people in its territories." Now, this would seem to be what I see from the directives, the directive that Talic himself pushed out, based on the first directive, was very detailed. He provided the detail. The strategic objectives were given to him at a higher level, and that there were also these oral assignments. Maybe this is a reflection on the type of meeting that we saw in the 3rd of June and the -- some of the meetings notated in Mladic's diary and the reference to the meeting in November that we just reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. In the time we have left we're now going to switch gears. We've gone through the directives and, in a way, phase two as it's described in the combat-readiness report. I would like to talk now more about military operations that began in the first phase, the early phase, and this is the military operations part of your report starting at page 60 in general where you identify common features of military operations conducted in the Bosanska Krajina 1KK zone. Those include weapons surrender dead-lines, co-operation of the military and the police or the MUP, retaliatory killings or killings of prisoners, the movement of the population, et cetera. So that's where we're going now. The area which you talk about on your executive summary at page 7. And the first document I'd like to show is 09466, this is the 65 ter number. And that is the RS at the 15 April 1992 mobilisation order. If we can bring that up. It's a one-page document so English and the Serbian is the same. And I'm going to go through just a quick series of these documents which concern the mobilisation. This is the first one. It's referenced at footnote 116 of your report. Can you just quickly tell us about this document, why you included it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think it was important because when I was looking at some of the documents from the 5th Corps, 1st Krajina Corps, in April and May and the engagement of some of the forces there, it seemed to me that in -- that there was a chain of documentation that was linked to some of the municipalities, whereby operations were undertaken to -- to get people to surrender illegally -- they called them illegally held weapons and those then manifested themselves in planning at municipal level, involving the police and the military, and subsequently engaged -- they were engaged in combat operations in those municipalities. And there's -- seemed to be a documentary chain in the ARK, at least for some of those municipalities, and this is one of the documents that was referenced at the beginning of that chain. And it was a mobilisation instruction from the Presidency declaring an imminent threat of war and the mobilisation of the TO -- in essence, the Serb TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Following on could we please have P02412.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, I have to keep intervening. This is not an instruction. This is a decision. It should be clarified and there are many such imprecisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it says "decision," we see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the transcript, it's "instruction," line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask, Mr. Brown, it does say "decision," doesn't it --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it's a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P02412, please, this is already an exhibit. It's dated the 16th of April, another decision signed by Minister of Defence Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This features several places in your report. Can you tell us about this document and it's relationship to the one we just saw and the one that we're going to see, the ones which followed.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this would clearly be linked to the previous decision and at the ARK, autonomous region level they've taken that decision and are passing that down their own chain. It talks about the Presidency decision of the 15th of April and they say that the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic shall be formed as the armed force and that other decisions relating to components of the armed force shall be made in keeping with the solution on the political organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the state -- statute, maybe status, of the JNA. So this was in this period when it wasn't exactly clear what was going to happen to the JNA. If I take you to the second page, paragraph 3 states: "The declaration of an imminent threat of war implies taking all the necessary measures stemming from the situation, and in keeping with the specific situation in the given territory." And the last sentence reads: "In preparation for the instruction as well as the engagement of TO units, achieve co-operation with JNA units, and where possible, put them under a single command." So it seems to be taking the presidential decision of an imminent threat of war and passing that down to the -- down the chain, in essence, establishing the Serb TO and allowing them to take necessary measures in relation to, presumably, their municipalities or areas that they're operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, P02818, this is the 4th of May, 1992, Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, Regional Secretariat for National Defence, signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sajic. And can you tell us about this document, how it relates to the one we just saw and later documents we'll see about disarmament dead-lines.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this one seems to be the next one in the chain. The measures that they're taking pursuant to a decision 192 of the 16th of April, it's -- potentially be the one previous. They're issuing the -- a dead-line, talking about mobilisation. But in paragraph 5 they're talking about a dead-line, which states that: "All paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possess weapons and ammunition are hereby urged to present themselves no later than 1500 hours on the 11th of May, 1992, to the municipal Territorial Defence staffs or the nearest public security stations. After the expiry of this dead-line, the competent authorities will conduct searches for weapons and ammunition applying the strictest measures." So it may well be that the previous decision they believe authorises them to take this kind of measure and they're issuing a dead-line in the municipalities for a surrender of they call illegally held weapons and that strict measures will be taken to those who -- well, it says that competent authorities will conduct searches after the expiration of the dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It also, I think at the end of the document, notes the presence of the Councils for National Defence shall be held responsible for implementing the decision. So it's clear there's an expectation that down at the municipal level these types of operations are to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if it is convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the Chamber will rise for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I make one point, Your Honours. I failed to ask to admit, when we started talking about directive four documents and whether to go through them, 14815, to tender that, if I may, that was the preparatory or warning order which Mr. Brown discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 14815 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will be well aware, Mr. Brown, that you are not supposed to discuss with the parties or anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of November, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
